items.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S8158

SPONSOR: KENNEDY
 
TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public authorities law, the highway law, the trans-
portation law and the vehicle and traffic law, in relation to renaming
the Thomas E. Dewey Thruway to the Frederick Douglass Thruway

 
PURPOSE:

This legislation would rename the New York State Thruway the Frederick
Douglass Thruway.

 
SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section one amends the closing paragraph of section 356 of the public
authorities law, as added by chapter 23 of the laws of 1964 to rename
the New York State Thruway the Frederick Douglass Thruway.

Section two amends the paragraph I of subdivision 31 and paragraph 7 of
subdivision 34 of section 341 of the highway law, paragraph 1 of subdi-
vision 31 as amended by chapter 594 of the laws of 1988 and paragraph 7
of subdivision 34 as added by chapter 550 of the laws of 1985 to rename
the New York State Thruway the Frederick Douglass Thruway.

Section three amends section 342-d of the highway law to rename the New
York State Thruway the Frederick Douglass Thruway.

Section four amends section 343-s of the highway law, as added by chap-
ter 277 of the laws of 2005 to rename the New York State Thruway the
Frederick Douglass Thruway.

Section five amends section 33 of the transportation law, as added by
chapter 420 of 7 the laws of 1968 to rename the New York State Thruway
the Frederick Douglass Thruway.

Section six amends subdivision 2 and paragraph (k) of subdivision 3 of
section 1180-a of the vehicle and traffic law, as amended by chapter 464
of the laws of 2003 to rename the New York State Thruway the Frederick
Douglass Thruway.

Section seven establishes that the commissioner of transportation shall
provide for the installation and maintenance of adequate signing of the
state highway system

Section eight establishes the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

This bill aims to honor Frederick Douglass. Douglass was one of the most
eminent human rights leaders of the 19th century. His oratorical and
literary brilliance thrust him into the forefront of the U.S.  abolition
movement, and he became the first black citizen to hold high rank in the
U.S. government.

Douglass was separated as an infant from his enslaved mother and lived
with his grandmother on a Maryland plantation until he was eight years
old when his owner sent him to Baltimore to live as a house servant with
the family of Hugh Auld, whose wife defied state law by teaching him to
read. Upon the death of his master, he was returned to the plantation as
a field hand at age 16. Later he was hired out in Baltimore as a ship
caulker. Frederick tried to escape with three others in 1833, but the
plot was discovered before they could escape.

Five years later, Douglass was able to flee to New York City and then to
New Bedford, Massachusetts, where he worked as a laborer for three
years, eluding slave hunters by changing his surname to Douglass.
Distinguished for his oration, he quickly became a prominent abolition-
ist leader and lecturer. Following the publication of his autobiography
in 1845, Douglass traveled to England, where he lectured on the American
anti-slavery movement and raised funds that purchased his legal freedom.
An oft-quoted dictate of his was: "If there is no struggle there is no
progress."

Douglass lived in Rochester from 1847 to 1872 - living in Rochester
longer than he lived anywhere else during his lifetime. It was in
Rochester that he began publishing his newspapers, The North Star and
Frederick Douglass' Paper, in which he endorsed women's suffrage, and
continued to aid the "underground" flight of slaves to freedom.  During
his years in Rochester, Frederick Douglass was an important part of many
triumphs in the abolition of slavery and the women's suffrage movement.
In 1872, he became the first African American to be nominated for Vice
President of the United States. Though he did not win that election, he
continued to work tirelessly for social reform until his death in 1895.
After he died, Douglass was buried in Rochester's historic Mount Hope
Cemetery, which is also the final resting place of suffragist Susan B.
Anthony.

In 1848, he attended the Seneca Falls Convention in Upstate New York.
He was the only African American to attend the first women's rights
convention. His powerful words helped to pass the resolution for women's
suffrage.

The renaming of the New York State Thruway after Frederick Douglass is a
fitting tribute to a man who changed American history and was a key
figure in New York's ascension as a center for abolitionist movements
and women's rights.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New legislation

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

To be determined.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
The thirtieth day after it shall have become a law
